# go-simple

The **Go-Simple** project is a dynamic, open-source **Golang** 💻 repository that serves as a modern **blueprint** for building **scalable, clean, and production-ready web services** 🚀. It showcases best practices in architecture by strictly adhering to **Clean Architecture** 🏗️ and **domain-centric modularity**, organizing code into distinct layers (controllers, services, and repositories) to ensure the application is highly **maintainable** ✅ and easily **testable** 🧪 as it grows.

---

### ✨ Key Architectural Features

* **Dependency Management:** Uses **Uber FX** ✨ for robust dependency injection and graceful application lifecycle management.
* **Web Framework:** Leverages the **Gin** framework 🌐 for a high-performance HTTP layer.
* **Data Access:** Utilizes **SQLC** 💾 for type-safe interaction with the database.
* **Performance:** Integrates a **Redis-backed cache layer** 🧠 for speed and efficiency.
* **Communication:** Includes a **gRPC server** ⚡ to demonstrate high-performance microservice communication.
* **Core Module:** Features a fully functional **Product Management Module** 📦 with complete **CRUD** (Create, Read, Update, Delete) functionality.

---

### 📚 Documentation & Learning

This repository is an **evolving guide** to advanced Go development. All architectural decisions and feature implementations are thoroughly documented through a series of dedicated articles on Medium. By following this project, you can learn essential **advanced Go idioms**, master the use of **DTOs** (Data Transfer Objects) 💼, and implement professional-grade backend systems 💡.

[medium.com/list/gosimple-b350f5c3bdb6](https://mobinshaterian.medium.com/list/gosimple-b350f5c3bdb6)

go run cmd/server/main.go

## Swagger address

http://127.0.0.1:4000/swagger/index.html#/

## Generate Swagger Documentation

swag init --parseDependency --parseInternal -g cmd/server/main.go


## Run docker compose

docker compose up -d

## SQLC Generator

```
sqlc generate
```

## Run tests

```
go test ./test/server_test.go

```

## Run Sonar

```
docker run --name sonarqube \
  -p 9000:9000 \
  sonarqube:latest


go test -coverpkg=./... -coverprofile=coverage.out ./test

go test ./... -json > report.json

go tool cover -func=coverage.out
```



## Add sonar test

```
sonar-scanner \
  -Dsonar.projectKey=go-simple \
  -Dsonar.sources=. \
  -Dsonar.host.url=http://127.0.0.1:9000 \
  -Dsonar.token=sqp_XXXX
```

## Run project

```


## Generate Proto

```
protoc -I.   --go_out=. --go_opt=paths=source_relative   --go-grpc_out=. --go-grpc_opt=paths=source_relative   --grpc-gateway_out=. --grpc-gateway_opt=paths=source_relative   api/proto/product/v1/product.proto

npm install -g @liara/cli

liara deploy
```

docker run -p 4000:4000 --env-file .env go-simple:latest

```

# go-wordpress-extraction: product extraction service A stateless HTTP service that extracts one product from one product page. A client application sends a product URL with an API key. The service finds that site's parsing rules in a JSON file, fetches the page, and returns either the product or a structured root cause with evidence, in the same response. For sites behind bot protection that the service does not get past (lumens.com), a search engine (`duckduckgo`, `brave`, `mojeek`, `yahoo` or `yandex`) builds the product from the search result instead, without contacting the site. Whatever is found is returned, and every field that could not be found is listed in `unavailable_fields`. See [Search engines](#search-engines-duckduckgo-brave-mojeek-yahoo-yandex), [md/ENGINES.md](md/ENGINES.md) and [Responsible use](#responsible-use). For a shop that has no config at all, the AI crawler (off by default) is the default rule: it fetches the page and has an LLM read name, price, image, description, specs and features, each checked against the page. Two AI engines exist: `ai-crawler-avalai` (AvalAI, `deepseek-v4.1-flash`) and `ai-crawler-cloudflare` (Cloudflare AI Gateway, `@cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017`); `APP_DEFAULT_ENGINE` picks the one for shops without a config. After a few products it learns CSS selectors for the shop, so later requests need no LLM call. See [AI crawler](#ai-crawler-ai-crawler-avalai-ai-crawler-cloudflare), [md/AI_CRAWLER_AVALAI_PROPOSAL.md](md/AI_CRAWLER_AVALAI_PROPOSAL.md) and [md/AI_CRAWLER_CLOUDFLARE_PROPOSAL.md](md/AI_CRAWLER_CLOUDFLARE_PROPOSAL.md). There is no database and no Redis. Site configs and API keys are files that are re-read every 30 seconds. The design is in [md/SYNC_EXTRACTION_PROPOSAL.md](md/SYNC_EXTRACTION_PROPOSAL.md). Because nodes share nothing, you can run as many as you like. Each node reports how busy it is, so the client can act as the dispatcher and spread requests across nodes. See [Run distributed](#run-distributed-client-side-load-balancing). ```text POST /api/v1/extract X-API-Key {"url": "...", "request_id": "..."} GET /api/v1/sites X-API-Key enabled sites available for Copy it to each node, then compare the checksum each node logs on reload. - Site configs (`APP_SITE_CONFIG_DIR`). Use `GET /api/v1/sites` to check that each node serves the same versions. Limits are per node. `APP_MAX_CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` caps a single node, so the cluster's total capacity is the sum over all nodes. Nodes can have different capacities. Give larger machines a higher value. ### Endpoints for the dispatcher All of them need the client `X-API-Key` and respond with `Cache-Control: no-store`. | Endpoint | Returns | Use it for | |---|---|---| | `GET /api/v1/active` | `{"extract_active_requests": N}` | Cheapest check: how many extractions this node is running now | | `GET /metrics` | JSON `load` block plus counters | Full picture: capacity, free slots, busy sites, draining | | `GET /ready` | 200, or 503 while draining (public) | Taking a node out of rotation during a deploy | The `load` block of `GET /metrics`: ```jsonc "load": { "draining": false, // true: the node is shutting down; send it nothing "capacity": 8, // APP_MAX_CONCURRENT_REQUESTS "active": 3, // same number as /api/v1/active "available": 5, // capacity - active; 0 means the next request gets 429 "utilization": 0.375, // active / capacity "per_site_limit": 1, // APP_MAX_CONCURRENT_PER_SITE "sites_active": {"hmland": 1} // busy sites on this node } ``` `active` includes requests that are waiting for a busy site's slot on this node, not only requests that are fetching. ### Choosing a node 1. Poll every node every 1–5 seconds, and also after each response. Use `/metrics` if the nodes have different capacities. If they are all the same size, `/api/v1/active` is enough. 2. Remove any node that is `draining`, that fails to answer, or that has `available` at 0. 3. For a URL on site X, prefer nodes where `sites_active[X]` is below `per_site_limit`. On any other node the request waits up to `APP_SITE_WAIT_TIMEOUT`, then gets a 429. 4. From the rest, pick the node with the most `available` slots, or the lowest `utilization` when capacities differ. Break ties at random so the dispatchers don't all pick the same node. 5. Between polls, add one to the chosen node's count yourself, so a burst of requests doesn't all land on one node. 6. The numbers can change between your poll and your request. On a 429, read `Retry-After` and try another node. On a 503 (`SHUTTING_DOWN`), drop the node until `/ready` returns 200 again. ```go func pick(nodes []Node, site string) *Node { var best *Node for i := range nodes { n := &nodes[i] l := n.Load // from the last GET /metrics, plus requests sent since if n.Down || l.Draining || l.Available <= 0 || l.SitesActive[site] >= l.PerSiteLimit { continue } if best == nil || l.Available > best.Load.Available { best = n } } return best // nil: every node is busy; wait and poll again } ``` ### Things to know - **Politeness is per node.** Each node keeps its own `delay_ms` spacing and per-site limit. Three nodes crawling the same site can hit it three times as often. To stay gentle, send each site to one node, or lower the per-site settings. - **Retry the same request.** An extraction stores nothing, so you can resend the same request to another node after a 429, a 503, or a network error. - **Different exit IPs.** Give each node its own `APP_PROXY_HOST` and `APP_PROXY_PORT` to crawl from different addresses. - **Prometheus.** Scrape every node's `/metrics` with the `X-API-Key` header. Prometheus asks for the text format, so it gets the `extract_*` series. Cleaning, prompts, grounding, the cache, learning and metrics are shared; what differs (base URL, auth headers, extra headers, error mapping, request-id header) is a provider profile in `internal/aicrawler/provider.go`. There is no fallback from one engine to the other. The Cloudflare engine sends `cf-aig-skip-cache: true` (this service caches answers itself), `cf-aig-metadata` (host, purpose, prompt version) and, by default, `cf-aig-no-wholesale: true` and `cf-aig-collect-log: false`. It does not send the gateway's retry headers: the SDK already retries. - **Cost on `/metrics`.** Every call to the AI provider is counted, including the one repair call after a non-JSON answer and the selector-learning calls. The JSON report has an `ai` block (`calls`, `failed`, `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_hits`, and one `series` entry per engine, model, purpose, host and outcome). The Prometheus text has `extract_ai_calls_total`, `extract_ai_tokens_total{kind="input|output"}`, `extract_ai_call_seconds_total` and `extract_ai_cache_hits_total`, labelled with `engine`, `model`, `purpose` (`extract`, `repair`, `learn`), `host` and `outcome` (`ok` or the `AI_*` code). Counters start at 0 when the process starts; use Prometheus `increase(extract_ai_tokens_total[1d])` for tokens per day. Because the default rule accepts any domain, only the first 200 hosts get their own label and the rest are counted as `other`. The `engine` label was added with `ai-crawler-cloudflare`: dashboards that sum these series must add `engine` to their `sum by (...)`, or sum over it. - **Default rule.** With `APP_AI_CRAWLER_ENABLED=true`, a URL whose host has no file in `configs/sites/` and no active learned config is served by the built-in rule `ai-crawler-default` (`config_origin: default`) with the engine `APP_DEFAULT_ENGINE` names, instead of failing with `SITE_NOT_CONFIGURED`. A site config always wins, then an active learned config. `config_version` is `builtin-1` with AvalAI and `builtin-1+cloudflare` with Cloudflare. `GET /api/v1/sites` lists the rule last, with `domains: ["*"]`, the engine and its model, sets `accepts_any_domain: true` and names the engine in `default_ai_engine`. `APP_DEFAULT_ENGINE=none` turns the rule off. - **Per site.** A config can set `"fetch": {"engine": "ai-crawler-avalai"}` or `"ai-crawler-cloudflare"`, or `"engine": "default"` to follow `APP_DEFAULT_ENGINE`; it then needs no `root` or `fields`. `"ai_fetch": "web_search"` (AvalAI) never contacts the site: only the URL goes to `APP_AI_CRAWLER_SEARCH_MODEL`, at least one cited source must be on the site, and the values are unverified (see [md/ENGINES.md](md/ENGINES.md) section 3.7). An engine that is not configured on the instance gives `ENGINE_UNAVAILABLE`. `"locale": {"price_unit": "auto"}` reads the currency from each page, and `"fetch": {"ai_fetch": "browser"}` always renders in Chrome. - **Pipeline.** The page is fetched with the `http` engine. A JavaScript shell is rendered once in Chrome when `APP_BROWSER_ENABLED=true`; otherwise it fails with `JS_RENDERED_PAGE`. The HTML is cleaned (title, meta, JSON-LD and visible text; scripts, header, nav, footer and hidden elements removed) and sent to `POST {APP_AI_CRAWLER_BASE_URL}/chat/completions` with the official [`openai-go`](https://github.com/openai/openai-go) SDK. The model returns JSON: `name`, `price` (copied text), `url`, `image`, `description`, `specs`, `features`. - **Grounding.** Every value must appear on the page: the name and spec texts in the page text, the image among the page's image URLs, each price amount among the page's amounts (parsed by the Go price parser, never by the model), and at least 60 % of the description's words. A value that fails is dropped and listed in `unavailable_fields` with reason `AI_NOT_GROUNDED`. Every AI result carries the warning `AI_EXTRACTED`; `source` adds `model`, `prompt_version`, `fetched_with` and `tokens`. - **Failures.** `AI_UNAVAILABLE`, `AI_RATE_LIMITED`, `AI_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`, `AI_AUTH_FAILED`, `AI_INPUT_TOO_LARGE`, `AI_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE` (wrong model, route or region) and `AI_BAD_OUTPUT` (after one repair request), with `evidence.ai` (model, provider, provider request id, HTTP status, provider code, tokens, and for Cloudflare `gateway_cache`). For Cloudflare the request id is `cf-aig-log-id`, the id to search for in the Cloudflare dashboard, and the provider code is Cloudflare's numeric code (`2009`, `2044`, ...). Keys and tokens are never in a response or a log. - **Selector learning.** After a successful AI extraction on a host without a config, the model is asked once for CSS selectors. They are kept only if the normal selector pipeline gives the same product on the same page, and are written to `configs/learned/.json` as a `candidate`. Later AI requests for the host also run the selectors in shadow; after `APP_AI_CRAWLER_LEARN_PROMOTE_AFTER` (3) different pages match, the config becomes `active` and serves the host with no LLM call (`config_origin: learned`, warning `LEARNED_CONFIG`). Learning calls use the default engine, and the learned file records it in `learned.engine`. When learned selectors fail, that request is answered by the default engine (or, with `APP_DEFAULT_ENGINE=none`, the engine that learned them; warning `LEARNED_CONFIG_FAILED`); 3 failures in a row demote the config and the host is learned again. Review learned configs with `go run ./cmd/sitectl learned list|show|activate|reject|adopt` (or `sudo ./deploy.sh learned ...`); `adopt` moves one into `configs/sites/`. - **Setup.** `sudo ./deploy.sh ai enable avalai` or `sudo ./deploy.sh ai enable cloudflare` on a server (asks for the key or token without echoing it and writes `secrets/avalai_api_key` or `secrets/cloudflare_api_token`), then `sudo ./deploy.sh default-engine` (lists the engines in recommended order and asks; or pass `ai-crawler-avalai`, `ai-crawler-cloudflare` or `none`). `sudo ./deploy.sh ai disable avalai|cloudflare` turns one engine off. Locally, `./menu.sh` item 7 sets up the engines and item 9 sets up the default engine from the same recommended list. `deploy.sh restart` and `menu.sh` "Run server" check `APP_DEFAULT_ENGINE` first, so a default engine that is not configured is reported before the server refuses to start. `deploy.sh` and `menu.sh` rewrite a leftover `APP_AI_CRAWLER_DEFAULT_RULE` into `APP_DEFAULT_ENGINE`. Keep secrets out of `.env.development` and `.env.test`: they are committed. - **Cloudflare billing.** The default model runs on Cloudflare (Workers AI, "Zero data retention"): no DeepSeek key, billed to the account (Workers Paid plan or AI Gateway credits; not on Workers Free), $0.30 per M input and $1.20 per M output tokens, about $0.0036 per product page. The token needs "Workers AI Read" as well as "AI Gateway Run". ### Response: completeness and unavailable_fields For every engine, the response returns whatever product data was found and lists every field that was not in `unavailable_fields` (an array in the JSON body; the HTTP status stays 200). The fields checked are `image_url`, `description`, `price`, `availability` and `specs` (and `title` when a failed result carries `partial.product`): | Reason | Meaning | |---|---| | `NOT_ON_PAGE` | The page was fetched, but the field was not on it (`http`, `browser`) | | `NOT_IN_SEARCH_RESULTS` | The search result does not include it (`duckduckgo`, `brave`, `mojeek`, `yahoo`, `yandex`) | | `NOT_CONFIGURED` | The site config does not extract it for this site | | `AI_NOT_GROUNDED` | The AI crawler returned a value that is not on the page, so it was left out (`ai-crawler-avalai`, `ai-crawler-cloudflare`) | `completeness` is `full` when the list is empty and `partial` otherwise. The existing `FIELD_MISSING` and `PRICE_MISSING` warnings are unchanged. ### Installing Playwright (browser engine) The browser engine requires Node.js, the driver pinned by `go.mod` (`playwright-go v0.6401.0` uses Playwright **1.64.1**), and the matching browser build. Playwright added Ubuntu 26.04 support in 1.61.0. [Playwright release notes](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/releases/tag/v1.61.0) If the machine reaches the internet through a proxy, export it first. Node.js, npm, Go and the browser download all use it: ```bash export https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:3067 export http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:3067 ``` **On a server, with deploy.sh (recommended).** `install` asks whether to enable the browser engine; on an existing server use `browser enable`. It installs Node.js, the driver and Chromium into `/opt/go-wordpress-extractor-playwright`, installs Chromium's system libraries (Debian/Ubuntu), writes `APP_BROWSER_*`, `PLAYWRIGHT_DRIVER_PATH` and `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` into `.env.production`, and checks that the browser starts as the service user. `-E` keeps the proxy variables through sudo. ```bash sudo -E ./deploy.sh browser enable # install Playwright + Chromium and turn the engine on sudo -E ./deploy.sh restart # apply sudo ./deploy.sh browser # status: enabled?, driver version, installed browsers sudo -E ./deploy.sh browser install # reinstall or update without changing settings sudo ./deploy.sh browser disable # turn off (files stay) ``` **Server without a screen (Xvfb).** Some pages only load in Chrome with a window, because headless Chrome is detected more often (for example, it stays on Cloudflare's "Just a moment..." page). On a server, that window is drawn on Xvfb, a virtual display in memory (no monitor or GPU, about 20-50 MB RAM). `browser enable` asks "Run Chrome in a window on Xvfb?" (default yes). With yes it sets `APP_BROWSER_HEADLESS=false`, installs Xvfb (`apt-get install -y xvfb`), checks that Chrome starts in a window on a temporary display, and adds a second systemd unit, `go-wordpress-extractor-xvfb`, that runs the display `:99`. The server unit requires it and gets `DISPLAY=:99`. Xvfb runs as its own unit instead of `xvfb-run` around the server, so a stop still sends SIGTERM to the server and running requests finish. To do the same by hand: ```bash sudo apt-get install -y xvfb # .env.production APP_BROWSER_ENABLED=true APP_BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome APP_BROWSER_HEADLESS=false # then let deploy.sh write both units and restart sudo ./deploy.sh service && sudo ./deploy.sh restart sudo ./deploy.sh browser # shows "window: Chrome runs in a window on Xvfb :99 (service ...: active)" ``` `sudo ./deploy.sh run` (foreground, no systemd) starts the server under `xvfb-run` when there is no display. Cloudflare also scores the server's IP address: a data-center address can still be challenged where a home connection passes, so test the site from the server itself. `sudo -E ./deploy.sh update` also updates the driver when `go.mod` moves to a new playwright-go version. Use `APP_BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome` (asked by `browser enable`) to install and use Google Chrome instead of Playwright's Chromium (x86_64 only). **On a development machine, by hand.** Use Node.js 22 or newer (`node --version`). This puts the driver where playwright-go looks by default, so tests and `go run ./cmd/server` find it without extra variables. ```bash PW_VERSION=1.64.1 D=~/.cache/ms-playwright-go/$PW_VERSION mkdir -p "$D" && cd "$(mktemp -d)" npm pack "playwright-core@$PW_VERSION" --silent tar -xzf "playwright-core-$PW_VERSION.tgz" -C "$D" ln -sf "$(command -v node)" "$D/node" "$D/node" "$D/package/cli.js" --version # Version 1.64.1 "$D/node" "$D/package/cli.js" install chromium chromium-headless-shell sudo "$D/node" "$D/package/cli.js" install-deps chromium # system libraries, Debian/Ubuntu cd - ``` Then run the server with the engine on, and the browser tests (they skip when Playwright is missing): ```bash APP_BROWSER_ENABLED=true go run ./cmd/server go test ./internal/fetch/ ./test/e2e/ -run 'Browser|Gate|Router|Engine' -v ``` With Google Chrome already installed you can skip the Chromium download and set `APP_BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome`. **In Docker.** `docker build --target runtime-browser -t go-wordpress-extractor:browser .` builds an image with all of the above. Behind a proxy on the host: ```bash docker build --network=host \ --build-arg https_proxy=$https_proxy --build-arg http_proxy=$http_proxy \ --target runtime-browser -t go-wordpress-extractor:browser . ``` ## Swagger Swagger UI: http://127.0.0.1:4000/swagger/index.html (operator credentials required). The doc is generated from the `@` annotations on the handlers and the struct tags of the request and response types, as before: ```bash go install github.com/swaggo/swag/cmd/swag@latest swag init --parseInternal -g cmd/server/main.go -o docs ``` Regenerate after changing an annotation or an API type. Generate a client from `docs/swagger.json`: ```bash openapi-generator-cli generate -i docs/swagger.json -g typescript-axios -o ./extract-client ``` How set admin for swagger APP_OPS_USER=admin APP_OPS_PASSWORD_HASH= ```bash echo 'choose-a-long-password' | APP_API_KEY_PEPPER=$(grep '^APP_API_KEY_PEPPER=' .env.development | cut -d= -f2-) go run ./cmd/apikey hash-ops-password ``` ## Tests ```bash go test ./... # unit, fixture, contract, and end-to-end tests go test -race ./test/e2e/ # end-to-end only go test -coverpkg=./internal/... -coverprofile=coverage.out ./... && go tool cover -func=coverage.out ``` The end-to-end suite starts the real Fx application on a free port with temporary config and key files, and points it at a local fake shop. A test resolver maps hostnames such as `shop.test` to that shop, so redirects, SSRF checks, TLS errors, and DNS failures are all exercised without the internet. It covers every failure code, every price state, request validation, authentication, capacity and per-site limits, per-site delay, cancellation, deadlines, draining, operator endpoints, HTTPS, hot reload of keys and sites, and the `apikey` CLI. Every response in the suite is validated against the generated Swagger doc, and properties missing from it fail the test. `TestSwaggerDocsUpToDate` fails when `docs/` was not regenerated after an annotation or type change (it is skipped if `swag` is not installed). ## Docker ```bash export APP_API_KEY_PEPPER=... # the pepper used to hash secrets/.env.apikeys docker compose up --build # service on :4000; configs/ and secrets/ are mounted read-only docker compose --profile tools up sonar # optional SonarQube ``` The key file is mounted rather than passed with `--env-file`, so revocations apply without a restart. `stop_grace_period` is 190s so running requests can finish. ## Sonar ```bash go test -coverprofile=coverage.out -coverpkg=./internal/... ./... sonar-scanner -Dsonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000 -Dsonar.token= ```

projects.readme:
# mobinshaterian.com

Personal portfolio and technical blog for Mobin Shaterian. The site presents a resume-style home page and a searchable archive of 200+ articles imported from Medium.

The application is built with React and TanStack Start, then pre rendered to static HTML for deployment to GitHub Pages. Blog content is stored as JSON in the repository, so the site does not need a database, CMS, or production API.

## What the site contains

- `/` — portfolio page with profile, experience, skills, education, recent writing, and contact details
- `/blogs` — full blog archive with tag filters and client-side full-text search
- `/blog/:slug` — an individual article rendered from local JSON
- `/data/posts-index.json` — public, machine-readable post metadata
- `/data/posts/:slug.json` — public JSON representation of an article
- Custom application and article 404 pages
- SEO metadata, Open Graph fields, canonical Medium links, and article JSON-LD

## Technology stack

### Application framework

| Technology                                            | Purpose in this project                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [React 19](https://react.dev/)                        | Builds the user interface from components.                                                                                                                   |
| [TypeScript](https://www.typescriptlang.org/)         | Adds static types to the React and server code. Strict mode is enabled.                                                                                      |
| [TanStack Start](https://tanstack.com/start/latest)   | Full-stack React framework responsible for server rendering, application startup, and prerendering.                                                          |
| [TanStack Router](https://tanstack.com/router/latest) | Type-safe, file-based routing, route loaders, URL search parameters, metadata, 404 handling, and scroll restoration.                                         |
| [TanStack Query](https://tanstack.com/query/latest)   | Provides the application-level `QueryClient`. It is ready for cached asynchronous data, although the current pages mainly use local JSON.                    |
| [Vite](https://vite.dev/)                             | Development server, hot module replacement, and production build pipeline.                                                                                   |
| [Nitro](https://nitro.build/)                         | Server/build engine used by TanStack Start. The configured `node-server` preset produces the `.output` build, including `.output/public` for static hosting. |

### Styling and UI

| Technology                                           | Purpose in this project                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Tailwind CSS 4](https://tailwindcss.com/)           | Utility-first styling, loaded through the Vite plugin and `src/styles.css`.                                                                                         |
| [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/)                  | Project convention and configuration for reusable UI components. Components are copied into `src/components/ui`, rather than installed as a single runtime package. |
| [Radix UI](https://www.radix-ui.com/)                | Accessible primitives underlying the shadcn components.                                                                                                             |
| [Lucide React](https://lucide.dev/)                  | Icons used throughout the portfolio and blog pages.                                                                                                                 |
| `class-variance-authority`, `clsx`, `tailwind-merge` | Class composition, component variants, and conflict-safe Tailwind class merging.                                                                                    |
| Inter and JetBrains Mono                             | Web fonts used for the main text and terminal-inspired interface.                                                                                                   |
| `tw-animate-css`                                     | Reusable Tailwind animation utilities.                                                                                                                              |

The repository also includes shadcn components backed by libraries such as Sonner, Vaul, Recharts, Embla Carousel, React Hook Form, Zod, and React Day Picker. Many are available for future UI work and are not currently used by the three main pages.

### Content and search

| Technology                                          | Purpose in this project                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| JSON files                                          | Store profile details, post metadata, full post content, and the search corpus.                             |
| [MiniSearch](https://lucaong.github.io/minisearch/) | Runs full-text blog search entirely in the browser. The search index is fetched lazily when search is used. |
| [Zod](https://zod.dev/) and `@tanstack/zod-adapter` | Validate the `/blogs` URL parameters (`q` and `tag`).                                                       |
| [Cheerio](https://cheerio.js.org/)                  | Parses exported Medium HTML in the import script. It is a development dependency, not browser code.         |
| `slugify`                                           | Installed slug-generation utility; it is not currently referenced by the application or import scripts.     |

### Tooling and delivery

| Technology             | Purpose in this project                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [Bun](https://bun.sh/) | Package manager and command runner. `bun.lock` makes installs reproducible.                                              |
| ESLint 9               | Lints TypeScript, React hooks, and refresh-compatible exports.                                                           |
| Prettier               | Formats source and configuration files; formatting violations are surfaced through ESLint too.                           |
| GitHub Actions         | Builds the site on every push to `main` and deploys `.output/public` to GitHub Pages.                                    |
| GitHub Pages           | Static production host. `CNAME` and `public/CNAME` configure the custom domain.                                          |
| Lovable                | The project is connected to Lovable and uses its TanStack/Vite configuration package and browser error-reporting bridge. |

## How the application works

### Routing and rendering

Routes live in `src/routes` and follow TanStack Router's file-based conventions:

| Source file                 | Route                                                                 |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/routes/__root.tsx`     | Root document, global metadata, providers, error boundary, and 404 UI |
| `src/routes/index.tsx`      | `/`                                                                   |
| `src/routes/blogs.tsx`      | `/blogs`                                                              |
| `src/routes/blog.$slug.tsx` | `/blog/:slug`                                                         |

`src/routeTree.gen.ts` is generated from these files. Do not edit it manually.

At build time, `vite.config.ts` reads every slug from `src/data/posts-index.json` and adds the home page, archive, and all article URLs to the prerender list. TanStack Start and Nitro render those routes ahead of time. The resulting static site is written to `.output/public` and can be hosted without a running Node server.

The custom server entry in `src/server.ts` is still used by the build/server-rendering pipeline. Together with `src/start.ts` and the error helpers in `src/lib`, it converts catastrophic SSR failures into a user-friendly HTML error page and reports client-side route errors to Lovable when that bridge is available.

### Blog data flow

The content pipeline intentionally writes two copies of some data:

```text
Medium HTML export
        |
        v
scripts/import-medium.mjs
        |
        +-- src/data/posts/*.json --------> bundled by article route loaders
        +-- src/data/posts-index.json ----> home page, archive, prerender route list
        +-- src/data/search-index.json ---> source copy of the search corpus
        |
        +-- public/data/posts/*.json ------> public /data/posts/:slug.json files
        +-- public/data/posts-index.json --> public metadata endpoint
        +-- public/data/search-index.json -> browser full-text search
```

The copies under `src/data` are application source inputs. The copies under `public/data` are copied unchanged into the public build and can be fetched directly by browsers or other tools.

An article JSON file contains metadata plus an ordered `content` array. `PostContent.tsx` renders supported block types: headings, paragraphs, code, images, quotes, lists, embeds, and horizontal rules. Code blocks include a copy button; YouTube embeds render inline, while other embeds become external links.

On `/blogs`, titles and post cards come from the small metadata index. The larger search index is downloaded only after a visitor focuses the search field or supplies a query. MiniSearch gives titles and tags more weight than article body text and supports prefixes and fuzzy matches. The selected query and tag stay in the URL, so filtered views are shareable.

### GitHub Pages routing

Static hosts cannot normally resolve an unknown nested client-side URL. `public/404.html` stores the requested location in `sessionStorage` and redirects to `/`; the root React component then restores that path through TanStack Router. Pre rendered known routes load directly, while unknown routes reach the application's 404 UI.

## Local development

### Requirements

- Bun (the repository uses a Bun lockfile)
- A current Node-compatible environment; CI installs the latest Bun release

Install and start the development server:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash  # skip if Bun is installed
bun install
bun run dev
```

Vite prints the local URL, normally `http://localhost:3000`.

No environment variables, external database, or API credentials are required for the current site.

## Available commands

| Command             | Description                                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `bun run dev`       | Start the Vite development server with hot reload.    |
| `bun run build`     | Create the production/pre rendered build in `.output`. |
| `bun run build:dev` | Build using Vite's development mode.                  |
| `bun run preview`   | Preview the production build locally.                 |
| `bun run lint`      | Run ESLint and Prettier checks.                       |
| `bun run format`    | Rewrite supported files with Prettier.                |

There is currently no automated test command.

## Editing site content

Portfolio content is data-driven. Update `src/data/profile.json` to change the name, summary, contact details, skills, work history, or education. The home page reads that file directly.

Global colors, fonts, terminal effects, and reusable CSS utilities are in `src/styles.css`. The theme uses CSS variables with OKLCH colors and Tailwind's `@theme` mapping.

To add a route, create a file under `src/routes` using the conventions documented in `src/routes/README.md`. The route tree will be regenerated by the TanStack Router tooling.

## Importing articles from Medium

Medium articles are generated from the `posts` directory inside an unzipped Medium export:

```bash
bun scripts/import-medium.mjs /absolute/path/to/medium-export/posts
```

By default, the importer attempts to download article images into `public/blog-assets`. To retain the remote Medium image URLs instead:

```bash
DOWNLOAD_IMAGES=0 bun scripts/import-medium.mjs /absolute/path/to/medium-export/posts
```

The importer:

1. Ignores draft HTML files.
2. Extracts article metadata and canonical URLs.
3. Converts supported HTML elements into typed content blocks.
4. Estimates reading time at roughly 220 words per minute.
5. Preserves existing tags from `src/data/posts.json` when slugs match.
6. Writes matching source and public post collections and indexes.

After importing, run the normal validation commands and inspect the changed JSON before committing:

```bash
bun run lint
bun run build
```

Two one-off maintenance scripts are also included:

- `bun scripts/fix-images.mjs` maps missing `/blog-assets/...` references back to original Medium CDN images. It currently expects exported HTML at `/tmp/medium-ext/posts`.
- `bun scripts/retag-ml.mjs` scans article text and consistently adds or removes the `Machine Learning` tag across both source and public indexes.

Both maintenance scripts rewrite many generated JSON files, so review their diff before committing.

## Production deployment

Pushing to `main` triggers `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`. The workflow:

1. Checks out the repository.
2. Installs Bun.
3. Runs `bun install --frozen-lockfile`.
4. Runs `bun run build`.
5. Uploads `.output/public` as the GitHub Pages artifact.
6. Deploys that artifact to the `github-pages` environment.

For a manual deployment, run the workflow from the GitHub Actions interface. GitHub Pages must be configured to use GitHub Actions as its source.

## Important maintenance notes

- Keep `src/data` and `public/data` synchronized; the import and maintenance scripts already update both.
- Add new article slugs to `src/data/posts-index.json` through the importer so `vite.config.ts` pre renders them.
- Do not edit `src/routeTree.gen.ts` by hand.
- Do not commit `.output`, `dist`, `.vinxi`, or `node_modules`.
- This repository is connected to Lovable. Do not force-push, rebase, amend, or squash commits that have already been pushed, because rewriting published history can break Lovable's project history.


# Technology
- **React** – the actual UI library, same as what you know.
- **TanStack Start** – a full-stack React framework (like Next.js, but from the TanStack team — makers of React Query, TanStack Router). It adds file-based routing, server-side rendering, and API routes on top of plain React.
- **Vite** – the build tool/dev server. Fast hot-reload, bundles everything for production.
- **Nitro** – the server engine TanStack Start uses under the hood to actually run/deploy the server (handles the `node-server` preset in your `vite.config.ts`, and produces the static output in `.output/public`).
- **TypeScript** – your code is `.ts`/`.tsx`, typed React.
- **shadcn/ui** (implied by `components.json`) – a component library built on Radix UI + Tailwind CSS, pretty common in Lovable.dev-generated projects.
- **Pre rendering** – your `vite.config.ts` has `prerender.enabled: true` with a list of static pages (home, blogs, each blog post) — so at build time it crawls your routes and outputs static HTML, which is why this can deploy to GitHub Pages (a static host) instead of needing a live Node server.
- **bun** – package manager/runtime, replacing npm.
- **Lovable.dev plugins** (`@lovable.dev/vite-plugin-*`) – dev-time tooling from the platform this was originally built in (hot-reload bridges, etc.) — not something you'll need to touch for normal editing.
